LESSON MENU
PRINTED CIRCUIT BOARDS

Almost all electronic devices contain printed circuit boards or PCB's. These boards serve as the connection point for the circuit components. Printed circuit boards provide a much easier and reliable method of circuit connection than using individual wires from component to component.
DISCUSSION
0PHTITTI""U

A printed circuit board is basically a sheet of insulating material, also known as a baseboard, with copper foil bonded to one or both sides. The copper is used as the conducting path between components which are mounted on the board.

The baseboard is usually made of layered paper or glass laminates covered with epoxy or resin. These construction materials give the board high insulation resistance, good temperature stability, shock resistance and can also make them flame proof. These are all desirable characteristics for a PCB.
The copper foil which is bonded to a PCB is made of very pure copper, typically 98.5%. The purity of the copper ensures low resistance between connections and allows for good quality solder joints.

Most PCB's start with an entire layer of copper foil on one or both sides. These boards are typically called blanks. Once the circuit to be placed on the board has been designed, a template for the circuit paths is developed.

The template of the conductor paths is used in the manufacturing process to remove the extra copper from the board, leaving only the required conductor paths. These pathways, traces, act as connecting wires. This process is known as etching.

To make the most economical use of a circuit board, both sides of the board are typically etched with appropriate circuit paths. This is called a double-sided circuit board. re only mounted on one side, but can be connected to traces on both sides of the board.

In most instances the components are only mounted on one side, but can be connected to the copper pathways (traces) on both sides of the board. h layer. These are known as multilayer boards and require specialized tools and experience to be repaired.

Once a board has been etched, holes must be drilled in it so that the components can be mounted securely. With high volume PCB manufacturing, the etching and drilling processes are usually automated and computer controlled.ntrolled....
Older style boards often have copper paths or traces on one side only. These are known as single-sided boards. However, most boards today are double-sided.

In many newer electronic devices where space is at a premium and circuits are complex, the boards are layered together, with traces and sometimes components on each layer. These are known as multilayer boards and require specialized tools and experience to be repaired. '

Once the holes have been drilled in a PCB, it is ready to have components mounted on it. The copper foil is left in pads around the drill holes so there is enough surface area to securely solder the component to the copper trace.

When dealing with components that are mounted on single-sided boards, the pad is only bonded to the board on one side and the hole is drilled through the board. This is called an unsupported hole.nd must be treated carefully when being soldered, or the pad may come loose from the board due to excess heat.

Unsupported holes must be treated carefully when being soldered. If excess heat is applied the pad may come loose from the board. rted hole and must be treated carefully when being soldered, or the pad may come loose from the board due to excess heat.

In situations where a component lead, or a jumper is passed through the board to connect on both sides, there are a number of possible connection methods. The simplest of these involves passing the lead through the board and soldering it to pads on both sides of the board. (GRAPHICS TEXT) A JUMPER SOLDERED TO PADS ON BOTH SIDES OF A BOARDDDDDDDDD

A more reliable method of through-the-board connection is a plated- through hole. In this situation, the pads on either side of the board are connected by continuous copper plating or some type of eyelet that goes through the board. This is known as a supported hole. 1. The use of printed circuit boards or PCB's is a convenient and common method of connecting components in an electrical circuit.
2. Most PCB's are made of glass/epoxy laminates and covered with a thin layer of copper which is etched to form conducting paths.
3. PCB's can be single-sided, double-sided, or multilayer.

4. Holes are drilled into the circuit board to mount components on the board. Care must be taken when soldering components into, or removing components from the board, so excess heat does not damage the copper connection traces.

5. In double-sided boards, the components must sometimes be passed through the board and connected on both sides. This may be done using an unsupported hole or a plated- through hole. The plated- through hole is more reliable.
6. When attempting repair or modification of any printed circuit board, it is wise to try and make the work as good, or better in quality than the original board.

PC BOARD COMPONENT INSERTION

When building a project or repairing a piece of electrical equipment, we are often required to mount components on a printed circuit board. This is sometimes referred to as loading or stuffing the board.

However, component insertion into PCB's requires more than simply soldering the components to the board. There are several important steps which must be taken before any soldering is done.

It is convenient to illustrate the procedure for installing components by using an example. In this instance, we will use a resistor as the component that we wish to install on the printed circuit board.
We will assume that the circuit board on which the resistor is to be mounted has already been etched and drilled to accept components.

The first step in the installation process is to bend the leads of the resistor to fit into the drill holes of the board. There is a specific method for doing this, using either a lead former tool or rounded needlenose pliers.
Ordinary pliers should not be used to bend the resistor leads because we do not want to nick the wire, as a nick will reduce the mechanical strength of the lead....
The bends in the leads should be kept at least 1/8" away from the body of the component. This prevents mechanical stress from damaging the component body or the body/lead junction.

There are several possible types of mounting techniques used to install components on printed circuit boards. e most common of these are shown below.

STRAIGHT-THROUGH MOUNT - One of the most commonly used types of termination. Because it does not have any bends in the lead after it passes through the board it is the easiest type of termination to remove and replace.
DEFINITION
DEFINITION

FULL CLINCH MOUNT - This termination is mostly used when components are mounted in unsupported holes however, it can be used in supported holes. The bend in the lead helps to stabilize the component so it does not move during soldering.
DEFINITION
OFFSET PAD MOUNT - A variation of the surface mount. It is not uncommon to find that the pad where the lead is to be joined is some distance away from the hole.
DEFINITION
SEMI-CLINCHED MOUNT - A variation of the full clinched lead where the lead is bent at a 45
DEFINITION
SPADE MOUNT - After the lead is passed through the hole it is flattened. This keeps the component in place during soldering. Removal of a spade mounted component requires special procedures.
DEFINITION
SURFACE MOUNT - Holes are not drilled in the boards for surface mounting. Components leads are soldered directly to flat pads on the surface of the board.
While any of these methods may be used on mass-produced PCB's, the straight-through mount is most often used in repair or project work.

Before the component is installed on the circuit board, both the component leads and the solder pads should be cleaned. In most cases, an eraser does a good job of removing dirt and oxides from the metal surfaces.

Try not to touch the component leads or solder pads with your fingers, as oils from your skin can reduce the bonding strength of the solder joint. A good general rule is to keep all areas that solder will contact as clean as possible.

Once the component leads have been fed through the board, and it is seated in the right position, the leads should be clipped to the correct length. For a straight-through connection, the lead length that protrudes through the board should be no greater than the pad radius.

Once the leads have been cut to the correct length, solder can be applied to complete the connection. The soldering tip is touched to the lead and pad to heat the connection first, then solder is fed in from the other side. er is fed in from the other side.

Using the correct amount of solder on a joint requires practice. A connection may hold a range of solder amounts and still be acceptable. However, it is also possible to use too much or too little solder.

PC BOARD COMPONENT EXTRACTION

When a component fault occurs on a printed circuit board, the component must usually be replaced. It is important to examine the circuit board thoroughly before attempting replacement, so you have an idea of the component mounting, position, board make-up, etc..
DISCUSSION
The original installation method should determine the correct method of component replacement. Always try to install the new component to the same standards that the original component was installed.

Care must be taken when removing the damaged component from the circuit board. Even if the old component is to be discarded, we must try to maintain the integrity of the circuit board connectors and the board itself.

The first step in removing a component is to remove the original solder from the connection. This is done using either the solder vacuum or solder wick method. th of these methods have been covered in a previous lesson.

Ensure you check the drill hole to see if it is plated through. If it is not plated-through, solder removal should be fairly easy using a solder vacuum or solder wick. illed with solder, you must ensure that all solder has been removed before attempting to remove the component. When removing components from PCB's, you must monitor the amount of heat that is applied to the joint. Too much heat can easily damage the thin copper traces on the circuit board as well as the board material itself. A common rule of thumb is to apply heat to a desoldered connection for a maximum of three seconds only.

When doing any repair to a printed circuit board, you should be aware that manufactured boards are often covered with a protective coating. e coating may provide electrical insulation, protection against mechanical vibrations, or protect against humidity. There are many types of coatings and they can be difficult to remove for board repair.

We have briefly covered how to replace damaged components on printed circuit boards, but another common problem is how to replace damaged copper traces on the board.

If a component or part of a circuit is shorted on a PCB, the current flowing through the traces can pulse to a very high level. In this case, the current level often exceeds what the circuit traces can handle............

High current through the thin circuit traces may cause them to heat to a very high temperature. This heat can either melt the trace, or loosen the trace from the board. Either of these conditions must be repaired for the board to work properly.
In addition, a circuit trace that has been nicked and has a reduced cross-sectional area, or is damaged in any other way, must also be replaced.

The first step in repair of a damaged trace is to asses the damage and determine which method of repair to use. Depending upon the amount of damage, the old trace or parts of it, may have to be cut off and discarded.
There are several methods used to repair a damaged trace. Common methods are: underbonding, overbonding and wire jumps.......esraces. s, solder, and any other foreign materials.

The second step in all repair cases, is to ensure the damaged area is thoroughly cleaned of all coatings, solder, and any other foreign materials. A hole is drilled through each end of the broken traces. The holes should be just large enough to allow the jumper wire to pass through, but not wider than the trace itself.

The jumper wire is then cut to a length so that it can go through the board and up onto the trace ends. The wire ends should extend a minimum of 1/16" over the tinned trace ends when fully clinched. The wire ends are tinned and formed so that the wire bends are sharp but there are no wire nicks.
Once the wire is installed properly, it should be soldered in place. The solder connections should then be cleaned and the repair is complete.
The last type of circuit board repair that we will examine is the replacement of pads or terminals that have been lifted from the board.

This type of repair is straightforward if you have the correct repair materials. These repairs require both replacement pads and through-board eyelets. Most well equipped repair stations have a selection of these.
If a pad or eyelet has been damaged or is missing, the area must first be cleaned. The hole should then be redrilled to a slightly larger diameter.

The proper pad is then selected to fit the new hole diameter. Installation of the pad is best done by someone who is familiar with the repair. It involves bonding the pad to the board and soldering the trace end to the existing trace material. Consult the repair manual or with an experienced technician before attempting this repair.

In some cases, an eyelet is used to keep the new pad in place. Special tools are needed for setting an eyelet in place. This process is referred to as swaging and simply causes the eyelet to stay in place by expanding it to a pressure fit. You should talk to someone who has done this type of repair before if you are not familiar with the process.

It is important to do any PCB repair work to a level which meets or exceeds the original workmanship. These types of repairs require skill that comes with practice. The help of experienced technicians can be valuable when you first start to do PCB repairs. Do not be afraid to ask for assistance or advice.

2. Repair work should always be done to the standard set by the work or to an even higher standard, if possible.

3. To remove a component, we must first note how it is mounted. The solder should be removed using the wick or vacuum method. Then heat and pliers can be used to lift the component off the board. The maximum heating time should be no greater than three seconds.
4. Components should be replaced using standard component installation procedures. The board, traces, pads, etc. should be thoroughly cleaned before reinstallation is attempted.
5. Other common PCB repairs include resetting lifted traces using adhesives, or jumpering open traces using either the surface wire jumper method or the through-board jumper method.
6. The repair of lifted, damaged, or missing solder pads is common. To perform these repairs adequately, a technician must have access to a drill, pads and eyelets, and swaging tools.
7. Printed circuit board repair is a skill that can be developed with practice and assistance from experienced technicians.
